title: The Winning of Kinghood: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How Several Kings and High Dukes Tried and Failed to Pull the Sword Out of the Anvil, and How Arthur Tried It and Won._
When the morning of Christmas day came, many thousands of people of every rank, both noble and common, gathered in front of the cathedral to watch the trial of that sword.

A canopy of embroidered cloth in many colors had been spread above the sword and the anvil, and a platform had been built all around the block of marble. Close by, a throne had been set up for the Archbishop. He was to oversee the trial and make sure that everything was done fairly and with proper care.

By midmorning the Archbishop himself arrived in great state and took his seat on the high throne that had been prepared for him. His whole court of clerks and knights gathered around him, so that he made a very proud and splendid sight, full of courtly dignity.

Nineteen kings and sixteen dukes had gathered for the trial. Each of them was of such noble and high rank that he hoped to be proven that very day before the whole world to be the rightful king and overlord of all Britain. So after the Archbishop had settled on his throne, several of them came and demanded that he put the matter to the test at once. The Archbishop ordered his herald to sound a trumpet and call everyone who had the right to try the sword to come forward for that adventure. The herald did as the Archbishop commanded.

As soon as the herald had sounded his trumpet, the first of the kings came forward to try the sword. He was King Lot of Orkney and the Isles. Eleven knights and five esquires came with King Lot, so that he looked very noble in the eyes of all. When King Lot reached the place, he climbed onto the platform. First he bowed to the Archbishop, and then he laid his hands on the pommel of the sword in full sight of everyone. He bent his body and pulled on the sword with great strength. But he could not move the blade in the anvil even by the width of a hair. It stood as firm as the iron it was set in. After that first attempt he tried three more times, but still he could not move the blade in the iron. Then, having tried four times, he gave up and came down from the platform. He was filled with great anger that he had not succeeded.

After King Lot came his brother-in-law, King Urien of Gore, and he made his attempt in the same way that King Lot had done. But he did no better than the first king. After King Urien came King Fion of Scotland, and after King Fion came King Mark of Cornwall. After King Mark came King Ryence of North Wales, and after King Ryence came King Leodegrance of Cameliard. After him came all the other kings and dukes who have been named, and not one of them could move the blade. Some of these high and mighty lords were filled with anger that they had failed. Others were ashamed that they had failed before the eyes of everyone watching. But whether they were angry or ashamed, it did them no good at all.

When all the kings and dukes had failed in this adventure, the people there were astonished, and they said to one another, “How can this be? If all these kings and dukes of such high rank have failed, who can hope to succeed? Every man most worthy of this great honor has been here, and all have tried to draw the sword, and all have failed. Who is left to come after them and hope to succeed?”

The kings and dukes talked together in the same way. After a while six of the most worthy came forward. They were King Lot, King Urien, King Pellinore, King Ban, King Ryence, and Duke Clarence of Northumberland. They stood before the Archbishop’s throne and spoke to him like this: “Sir, all the kings and dukes of this realm have struggled before you to draw out that sword, and look! Not one of those who tried has succeeded. What can we think, then, except that the enchanter Merlin set up this adventure to bring shame and disgrace on all of us here, and on you, the head of the church in this realm? For who in all the world could hope to pull a sword blade out of a bed of solid iron? Look! It is beyond the power of any man. Is it not plain to see that Merlin has made a fool of us all? Now, so that this great crowd will not have been called here for nothing, we beg you in your wisdom to choose at once the one best fitted to be overlord of this realm, from among the kings gathered here. When you have chosen him, we promise to obey him in everything he commands. Truly, such a choice will be better worth our while than wasting time on this foolish task. No man in all the world can pull a sword out of an anvil.”

The Archbishop was deeply troubled, for he said to himself, “Can it be true that Merlin has deceived me, and made a fool of me and of all these kings and noble people? Surely this cannot be. Merlin is very wise, and he would not make a fool of the whole realm for the sake of so poor a joke as this. Surely he has some purpose in this that we know nothing about, since we are less wise than he. So I will be patient a while longer.” Having thought this over, he spoke aloud to the seven high lords. “Messires,” he said, “I still have faith that Merlin has not deceived us, so I ask you to be patient for one short while longer. Wait for the time it takes a man to count five hundred twice over. If no one comes forward to do this task by then, at your request I will choose one of you and proclaim him King and Overlord of all.” For the Archbishop believed that Merlin was about to name a king before them all at any moment.
Now we will leave these men and turn to Arthur and his father and brother.

Merlin had told those three to wait in their pavilion until he thought the time was right for them to come out. That time had now come, and Merlin and Sir Ulfius went to the pavilion of Sir Ector. Merlin said, “Arthur, get up and come out, for now the hour has come for you to try, before the whole world, the miracle that you performed in private not long ago.” So Arthur did as Merlin told him. He came out of the pavilion with his father and his brother, and look! He was like someone walking in a dream.

So the five of them went down toward the cathedral and the place of the trial. When they came to the crowd gathered there, the people made way for them, marveling and saying to one another, “Who are these people with the enchanter Merlin and Sir Ulfius, and where do they come from? For all the world knew Merlin and Sir Ulfius, and the people knew that something very extraordinary was about to happen. Arthur was dressed all in flame-colored clothing embroidered with silver thread, so that others in the crowd said, “Truly, that youth is very fair to look upon. Who can he be?”

But Merlin said nothing to anyone. He brought Arthur through the crowd to the place where the Archbishop sat, and the crowd made way for him so that he was not held back. When the Archbishop saw Merlin coming with these others, he stood up and said, “Merlin, who are these people you bring to us, and what is their business here?” Merlin said, “Lord, here is one who has come to try that sword over there.” The Archbishop said, “Which one is he?” and Merlin said, “This is he,” and he laid his hand on Arthur.

Then the Archbishop looked at Arthur and saw that the youth had a very handsome face, so his heart went out to Arthur and he loved him very much. The Archbishop said, “Merlin, by what right does this young man come here?” Merlin answered, “Lord, he comes here by the best right there is in the world. The one who stands before you dressed in red is the true son of Uther-Pendragon and of his lawful wife, Queen Igraine.”

The Archbishop cried out in great surprise. Those standing close by, who heard Merlin’s words, were so astonished that they could not tell what to think. The Archbishop said, “Merlin, what are you telling me? Until this day, who in all the world ever heard that Uther-Pendragon had a son?”

Merlin answered, “No one has ever known of it until now, except a very few. This is how it happened. When this child was born, the spirit of prophecy came upon me, and I saw that Uther-Pendragon would die before very long. So I feared that the King’s enemies would lay violent hands on the young child for the sake of his inheritance. At the King’s command, another man and I took the young child from his mother and gave him to a third man. That man took the royal child and has raised him ever since as his own son. There are others here who can swear that all this is true. The man who was with me when the child was taken from his mother was Sir Ulfius, and the man to whom the child was given was Sir Ector of Bonmaison. These two witnesses, who are above all reproach, will swear to the truth of what I have said, for here they stand before you to confirm my words.”
Sir Ulfius and Sir Ector said, “Everything Merlin has said is true, and we give our most faithful and sacred word of honor on it.”
The Archbishop answered, “Who could doubt the word of such honorable witnesses?” Then he looked at Arthur with a smile.
Then Arthur said, “Lord, do I have your leave to take hold of that sword?” The Archbishop said, “You have my leave, and may the grace of God go with you as you try.”

Then Arthur went to the block of marble and laid his hands on the hilt of the sword that was thrust into the anvil. He bent his body and pulled hard, and look! The sword came out with great ease and very smoothly. When he had the sword in his hands, he swung it around his head so that it flashed like lightning. After he had swung it three times around his head, he set the point against the face of the anvil and pressed down hard. And behold! The sword slid smoothly back into the place where it had stood before, and when it was halfway in, it held fast. In this way Arthur completed the marvelous miracle of the sword in the eyes of all the world.

When the people gathered there saw this miracle performed before their faces, they all lifted their voices together. They shouted so fiercely and with such a huge uproar that it seemed the whole earth rocked and trembled with the sound.

While they were shouting, Arthur took hold of the sword again, drew it out, swung it, and drove it back into the anvil. Then he drew it out a third time and did the same thing as before. In this way everyone there saw the miracle performed three times over.

All the kings and dukes who were there were filled with amazement. They did not know what to think or say when they saw someone who was little more than a boy do the very thing at which the best of them had failed. Some of them, having seen the miracle, were willing to accept Arthur because of it, but others would not. These withdrew and stood apart, and as they stood there they said among themselves, “What is this? Who can believe such a thing, that a beardless boy should be set before us all and made King and overlord of this great realm to rule over us? No! No! We will have none of him for our King.” Others said, “Is it not clear that Merlin and Sir Ulfius are lifting up this unknown boy so that they may raise themselves up along with him?” So these discontented kings spoke among themselves, and the most bitter of them all were King Lot and King Urien, who were related to Arthur by marriage.

When the Archbishop saw the discontent of these kings and dukes, he said to them, “What is this, Messires! Are you not satisfied?” They said, “We are not satisfied.” The Archbishop said, “What do you want?” They said, “We want a different sort of king for Britain than a beardless boy whom no one knows, and whose birthright only three men can vouch for.” The Archbishop said, “What of that? Has he not done the miracle that you yourselves tried and failed to do?”
But these high and mighty lords would not be satisfied. With angry faces turned away, they left that place, filled with rage.

But other kings and dukes came and bowed to Arthur and paid him honor, wishing him joy of what he had done. The foremost of those who came to him in friendship was King Leodegrance of Cameliard. All the crowd acknowledged him and pressed around the place, shouting so that it sounded like thunder.

All this while Sir Ector and Sir Kay had stood to one side. They were weighed down by sorrow, for it seemed to them that Arthur had suddenly been lifted so far above their rank that they could never hope to come near him again. Now he was of kingly importance and they were only common knights. After a while Arthur saw them standing there with downcast looks. He went straight to them, took each one by the hand in turn, and kissed each on the cheek. Then they were glad again to be raised up to him in this way.

When Arthur left that place, great crowds of people followed him, so that the streets were completely filled with people pressing close. The crowd kept loudly hailing him as the chosen King of England, and those nearest to him tried to touch the hem of his clothes. Arthur’s heart was lifted up with great joy and gladness, so that his soul took wing and flew like a bird into the sky.

That day, then, Arthur won the adventure of the sword and took up his birthright as king. May God bless every one of you, so that you too may do well in all you set out to do. Any man can be a king in whatever life he is given, if he can draw the sword of success out of the iron of circumstance. So when your own time of trial comes, I hope it goes for you as it went for Arthur that day. May you win success that fully satisfies you, with great glory and perfect happiness. Amen.
